newsitem.title: USA: U.S. school pays damages in abuse of gay student.
newsitem.headline: U.S. school pays damages in abuse of gay student.

text.p: A Wisconsin school district on Wednesday agreed to pay nearly $1 million to a former high school student for failing to protect him from harassment and abuse because he was gay.
The out-of-court settlement came hours after a federal court jury found officials of the Ashland, Wisconsin, School District liable for their inaction in the case of Jamie Nabozny, now 21.
The settlement was worked out by lawyers for both sides before a jury in the court of U.S. District Judge John Shabaz had begun deliberations on damages.

Peg Byron, communication director for the New York-based Lambda Legal Defence and Education Fund, which represented Nabozny, said the settlement called for $900,000 in damages and up to $62,000 in medical expenses.

"This is the first time a federal jury has had a chance to judge a school for its response to anti-gay violence. The entire country should learn a lesson from the results," said Patricia Logue of Lambda's office in Chicago.
"Countless gay kids have paid a high price for abuse. Now the tables have turned and it is prejudice that is costly," she said.

Nabozny claimed his right to equal protection under the law as provided for in the U.S. Constitution was violated because the school district failed to heed his complaints. He was verbally abused and said at one point two boy pushed him into into a urinal and urinated on him.
He tried to commit suicide and was diagnosed as suffering from depression and post traumatic stress disorder.

During his junior year in high school in 1993 he dropped out and moved to Minneapolis where he earned a high school equivalency degree. For a time he lived in New Jersey but has since moved back to Ashland with his parents.
"I feel like I have justice, and that this means justice for all other kids out there who aren't sure if they should stay in school or stay alive," Nabozny said in a statement released by Lambda.
